text: Nothing in Laura Jesson's week is designed to accommodate a second life. She shops in a nearby town, she comes home, she is bored in a way that has no vocabulary attached to it, and a chance acquaintance with a doctor hardens into a standing weekly appointment. Its record is heavy for something this quiet: Academy citations for the direction, the writing and the lead performance, a place among Palme d'Or winners and on TSPDT's thousand. The film itself is small on purpose. David Lean gives the two of them eighty-six minutes, and what they stand to cost is not scandal but the particular damage two careful people would do to households that have done nothing to deserve it. Almost all of it is transacted in tone of voice, in how much weight a remark about the hour can be made to carry.

The bet is that six months of phonetic drill can pass a Cockney flower girl off as a princess. Henry Higgins makes the boast, Colonel Pickering takes him up on it, and Eliza Doolittle moves into the professor's house only after money has changed hands between him and her dustman father. Anthony Asquith plays all of this as comedy, and the comedy is what allows the ledger underneath to stay visible. Ninety-six minutes, briskly cut, made in a country where an accent still settled in advance what a life could contain. The transformation does not stay on one side of the experiment. The Academy's recognition fell on the picture and on both leads, a Volpi Cup went to the actor, and the adaptation carries a citation of its own.

A prison guard takes up with the widow of a man whose execution he oversaw, and she does not know it. Everything after that runs on the gap. The audience carries what she does not. Marc Forster works in close quarters and few words, so the pressure gathers in ordinary exchanges while the withheld fact quietly accrues interest. The film is filed as romance, which is not wrong, though the working materials are grief and guilt: two people reaching for each other for reasons neither can afford to examine. The Academy cited the original screenplay, and the lead performance took prizes in Hollywood, London and Berlin. A hundred and thirteen minutes, and most of them are spent inside a silence that only one of the two people in it knows is there.

The organizer arrives from somewhere else; the risk stays with the people who live there. Martin Ritt builds the whole film on that asymmetry. Norma Rae works a southern textile mill under conditions the film presents as facts rather than as outrage, and when she becomes the union man's local partner she does it in a town where nearly everyone she knows draws a check from the same company. What stands to be lost is concrete: the job, the house, the standing among neighbors who would rather not be asked to choose a side. Just under two hours, very little plot machinery, and a great deal of persuasion conducted one person at a time. Its picture, its adaptation and its lead performance were all marked by the Academy, and it was later taken into the National Film Registry.

Deedee left the stage for a marriage and children; Emma stayed and became famous. Years later the two of them are in a room together again, and one has brought a daughter. The girl is invited into Emma's company and takes up with a young Russian dancer, which is enough to reopen an argument the women have been conducting silently since they were young. Herbert Ross treats dancing as work rather than as spectacle, and the Academy's citations for direction and photography went to a film largely about bodies doing a job. The National Board of Review called it the year's best. What the story is really counting is the price of a decision: who is still paying for one made young, and which resentments went unspoken because speaking them would have ended a friendship.

A man is offered a way out of a country about to close, and he gives the seat up in order to keep working. Dith Pran is an interpreter, which in a war means being the person who makes another man's reporting possible and appears in smaller type beneath it. Roland Joffé gives a long first movement to the daily mechanics of that job in Cambodia: the arrangements, the waiting, the calls placed while the U.S. Army packs up. It sits on the BFI's hundred best British films, and Academy honors reached the direction, the photography and a lead performance. What the length buys, across a hundred and forty-two minutes, is a working partnership solid enough to bear what the Khmer Rouge are bringing toward it.

Twenty-five minutes leaves room for one turn and no subplots. Sachiko is tired and low in a way that nobody around her has thought to ask about, and the answer the film offers is not a lesson but a white rabbit and a trip to the Land of the Moon. Animation lets the idea be literal: she is brought face to face with her true self, a girl who is well and glad of it, and the two of them share a frame. This Japanese short is listed among Caméra d'Or and Golden Leopard titles. Fairy tales state their morals plainly and spend their invention elsewhere, on the country the rabbit leads to and the self waiting in it, and at this length there is little else for the film to be.

The old words were hypochondria and black melancholia; the clinical one is asthenic syndrome, and what it names is a person who cannot stay awake inside their own life. Nikolai teaches pupils who have decided in advance that nothing said to them counts. Kira Muratova takes a hundred and fifty-three minutes over this, a length that obliges an audience to sit inside the condition rather than observe it from a distance. Indifference is the material here and not the mood: the subject is people who have stopped receiving one another, in a Soviet film made in 1990. It took a Silver Bear Grand Jury Prize and a Nika for best picture, and it is carried on TSPDT's thousand and on the BBC's list of films directed by women.

A provincial orchestra is a small kingdom, and in this one the man on the podium is also a husband: the ensemble's director is married to one of his violinists. Then a conductor with an international reputation comes back to Poland to take over the same players, carrying an old attachment to that violinist's mother and an intention to revive it with the daughter standing in for her. It took a Golden Shell, and its leading performance a Silver Bear. Andrzej Wajda sets the hierarchy and the marriage inside one room, where a grievance raised in either register is raised in both. The husband has personal and professional reasons to resent the visitor and no way to keep them apart. A hundred and one minutes, and much of the tension is settled by who defers to whom in front of the orchestra.

A prisoner from one war ends up running for his life across the Polish countryside, which is nobody's idea of a battlefield. Jerzy Skolimowski keeps the film on him and on nobody else: an escaped Taliban fighter, eighty-four minutes, pursuit and weather and hunger, and no arrangement by which an audience is spared having to go with him. The thriller here is the oldest kind, in which something is chasing something and the terrain does the deciding. A man who cannot explain himself to a single person he meets makes an efficient test of where sympathy comes from, and the film declines to soften him in order to earn it. Venice gave it a Grand Jury Prize and its actor a Volpi Cup; the photography took a European award; Poland named it the year's best film.

Godard wrote the synopsis himself, and it runs as a list: a couple, a quarrel, a dog that strays between town and country. The seasons pass, and then a second film begins that is the same as the first and is not. Sixty-nine minutes. Plot is not the operating principle; the working unit is the join, a phrase set against an image that refuses to illustrate it. Talk of the demise of the dollar and of truth in mathematics turns up in the middle of a domestic fight, and it is not a digression. The critical record is emphatic: a Jury Prize, best picture from the National Society of Film Critics, places on the BBC's century list and on IndieWire's list for the decade. The audience average sits at 5.8, and the distance between those two facts describes the argument the film starts.

The men on this patrol are volunteers, which means no wages, no backup, and no authority beyond what they can enforce themselves. Lu Chuan took the case from life: antelope poaching in the mountains of Tibet, and the small group that went after the poachers across country that treats everyone in it the same. It took the Golden Horse for best feature and the Golden Rooster for best picture, and it is listed among the hundred greatest Chinese-language films. Eighty-five minutes, filed as action, though a pursuit at that altitude is measured in days and in fuel rather than in chases. The moral clarity of the premise is the first thing the logistics begin to wear down, and that erosion is what the film is actually about.

A five-year-old chalks a word on the floor with his left foot, and a household that had already settled its expectations has to begin again. Jim Sheridan keeps Christy Brown inside the family that raised him, Irish and working class and crowded, and the film is less about an affliction than about who does the daily labor of taking a person seriously. His mother does most of it. What follows is a working life: paintings, poems, books, all of it made by a body that grants almost no cooperation. A hundred and three minutes, moving fast, declining the uplift the material keeps offering. The picture, its direction and its lead performance all drew Academy citations, and it appears on the BFI's hundred British films, a filing its own nationality complicates.

Four sisters, one house, and a war that has just ended somewhere off the page. George Cukor keeps to the domestic side of the 1860s, where the aftermath of the Civil War registers as household economy rather than as history. A story with no battles in it has to find its stakes in smaller denominations, and the film treats those as sufficient: what is worn, what is given away, who marries and on what terms. The scale is a choice and not a limitation. At a hundred and fifteen minutes there is room for four temperaments to be told apart properly. A Volpi Cup went to the leading actress, Academy citations went to the picture, the direction and the adaptation, and the National Board of Review put it among the year's ten.
